content: Fox-Fordyce disease is a chronic condition characterized by the obstruction of sweat gland ducts. This blockage leads to a secondary inflammatory response, which is nonbacterial in nature, caused by the accumulation of secretions and cellular debris within cysts. It is important to distinguish this condition from hidradenitis, which shares similarities but often involves secondary bacterial infections, resulting in the formation of pus-draining sinuses. Fox-Fordyce disease is a severe dermatological disorder that currently lacks universally curative treatments, making it a challenging condition to manage effectively. The disease is named after George Henry Fox and John Fordyce, who contributed to its identification and understanding. The primary treatment for Fox-Fordyce disease involves the surgical removal of the skin tissue containing the affected sweat glands. In some cases, radiation therapy may be employed, and antibiotics are used to mitigate the inflammatory response. For Fordyce granules, no treatment is typically necessary unless cosmetic removal of labial lesions is desired. Inflamed glands can be managed with topical clindamycin to reduce symptoms. When the affected tissue is surgically excised, recurrence of the disease does not occur. Although exceedingly rare, neoplastic transformation of the affected glands has been reported in the medical literature.
